title: Flex Direction
summary: Explains flex-direction, the main axis and cross axis, and why properties like flex-basis mean width in a row but height in a column. The exercise stacks a rainbow of divs vertically using inline-flex, flex-direction: column and a child-combinator selector for flex-basis.

concepts.heading: Default flow versus flex flow
points: Normal HTML flow stacks inline items along a line until space runs out and stacks block items top to bottom.
Once a container has display: flex, its children line up on a single row, left to right. This comes from the flex-direction property, whose default value is row.
Think of 'row' as the direction in which the next item is placed, not as the number of rows; a row-direction container visually looks like columns side by side.

concepts.heading: Main axis and cross axis
points: flex-direction defines the main axis: row gives a horizontal main axis (left to right); column gives a vertical main axis (top to bottom).
The cross axis is always perpendicular to the main axis: vertical for row, horizontal for column.
Axes matter because many flex properties work relative to them. flex-basis sets the initial size of an item along the main axis, so it acts like width in a row and like height in a column.
(Extra) The other values are row-reverse and column-reverse, which flip the order along the main axis.

concepts.heading: Container properties versus item properties
points: display, gap and flex-direction go on the parent (the flex container).
flex-basis goes on the children (flex items); putting it on the container does nothing.

Because the divs in the exercise share no class or element type and the HTML must not change, the children are targeted with the child combinator and universal selector: .container > *. The > only matches direct children, not grandchildren or deeper descendants; * matches any element.
This lesson deliberately leaves flex sizing details (grow, shrink, what happens when there is not enough room) for a later dedicated lesson.

code_examples.caption: Column direction with sized items
Same flex-basis in a row means width
code_examples.code:
.container { display: flex; flex-direction: row; }
.container > * { flex-basis: 100px; }  /* 100px wide */

task.name: Stack the rainbow vertically
task.starting_point: index.html with a div.container (already display: flex, gold border, white text) holding seven coloured divs (Red to Purple) with different classes. HTML must not be modified. A goal image shows tall items stacked top to bottom.
task.goal: Change the layout using CSS only so the colours stack vertically, each 100px tall, and the container is only as wide as its content.
steps: Add flex-direction: column to .container so items run top to bottom.
Notice the items now stretch the full page width; change display: flex to display: inline-flex so the container shrinks to its widest content.
Try flex-basis: 100px on .container and observe that nothing changes, because it is an item property.
Use the docs (child combinator and universal selector) to write .container > * and set flex-basis: 100px there.
Experiment: switch direction back to row, remove inline-flex, shrink the window, and compare.
task.expected_result: Seven coloured blocks stacked vertically, each 100px high, inside a gold-bordered box that is only as wide as the longest label.

pitfalls: Forgetting that flex-basis in a column controls height, not width.
Leaving display: flex so the column stretches the full page width.
Reference repo adds an author footer that is not part of the course.

playground.coverage: Tasks mirror the exercise exactly: inline-flex, flex-direction: column, container > * with flex-basis 100px. Uses numbered .box items instead of the rainbow.
gaps_and_ideas: Add the explicit main-axis / cross-axis explanation with a diagram; the s09-display-flex demo has an axis readout that could be reused here.
Add a step that sets flex-basis on the container first and shows nothing happens, to teach container vs item properties.
Mention the child combinator vs descendant combinator difference with a nested div example.
Add a 'no HTML changes' constraint and use differently-classed colour divs like the original.
Demo idea: toggle row/column and watch the same flex-basis change from width to height.
